title: Accessing Mesoscale Functional Organization from Standard Functional MRI Leveraging AI-Based Super-Resolution
abstract: Access to the fine-scale functional organization of the human brain is essential for understanding cognition and neurological disorders yet remains beyond the reach of conventional functional MRI (fMRI) because of its limited spatial resolution and contrast-to-noise ratio. To overcome this limitation, we developed f-LENNS (functional Localization Enhancement via Neural-Net-Sharpening), an artificial intelligence (AI)-based framework that enhances the effective spatial resolution of reconstructed fMRI magnitude images. The model was trained exclusively on high-resolution synthetic MRI data using extensive domain randomization and no adversarial or generative components. This approach enables robust out-of-the-box generalization (without retraining) to experimental datasets obtained with diverse acquisitions, while effectively curbing hallucination. Our experiments show that our publicly available model substantially improves the spatial fidelity of functional activation maps across multiple imaging paradigms and generalizes to a cohort of individuals with atypical brain function caused by amblyopia (lazy eye). F-LENNS consistently outperforms conventional resolution enhancement approaches, including interpolation-based upsampling and sharpening methods. These findings demonstrate that AI-driven super-resolution combined with domain randomization can overcome domain shifts arising from differences in MRI acquisition, enabling scalable, fine-scale functional brain mapping with widely available MRI hardware. Summary statement Precision functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) at the mesoscale is transforming our understanding of human brain functions by enabling the visualization of fine-grained functional organization in the human brain. Recent advances have shown that precision fMRI can reveal heterogeneous cortical architecture, resolve mesoscale processing streams underlying sensory perception, attention, and decision-making, identify functional alterations associated with neurological disorders, and help explain inter-individual variability in cognition. However, the widespread adoption of these approaches remains constrained by the limited availability of ultra-high-field MRI systems. Here, we introduce f-LENNS (functional Localization Enhancement via Neural-Net Sharpening), an artificial intelligence (AI)-based framework that broadens access to mesoscale functional neuroimaging by enhancing the effective spatial resolution of conventional fMRI. The model is trained exclusively on domain-randomized synthetic MRI data and generalizes to diverse datasets without retraining : f-LENNS can super-resolve data obtained with different acquisition parameters and at different magnetic field strengths (3T and 7T), while minimizing hallucination artifacts. F-LENNS substantially improves the detectability and spatial fidelity of fine-scale functional organization defined by stimulus-evoked activity and accurately recovers mesoscale functional patterns from conventional-resolution fMRI. Importantly, the same model generalizes to individuals with atypical brain function, revealing disorder-related functional abnormalities without data- or disease-specific retraining. Together, these findings demonstrate that domain randomization enables AI-based super-resolution models to overcome domain shifts arising from heterogeneous MRI hardware and acquisition protocols. Compared with conventional approaches, including interpolation-based upsampling, AFNI sharpening, and AI models trained on real functional and/or structural MRI data, f-LENNS consistently provides superior reconstruction of fine-scale functional organization. By enabling precision functional imaging in individual participants using widely available MRI systems, f-LENNS expands access to mesoscale brain mapping and represents an important step toward scalable, individualized functional neuroimaging and precision medicine.

title: Automated MRI-Based Segmentation of the Cranio-Cervical Venous System Using a Dedicated Deep Learning Pipeline
abstract: ABSTRACT PURPOSE To develop an automated magnetic resonance imaging based segmentation pipeline for the cranio-cervical venous system (CCVS), a complex anatomical network for which no dedicated segmentation tool is currently available. MATERIALS AND METHODS A retrospective single-center cohort of 194 contrast-enhanced cranio-cervical MRI examinations acquired between 2019 and 2024 was used. Manual reference segmentations were initially performed on 50 examinations using 3D Slicer. A nnU-Net v2-based segmentation model was then trained through an iterative process combining automatic segmentation, manual correction, and retraining. A dedicated intermediate model was developed to distinguish the vertebral artery from the surrounding vertebral venous plexus. Segmentation performance was assessed using the Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC). The complete processing pipeline was integrated into an open-source software application, VenousNetworkAnalyzer (VNA). RESULTS The final model achieved a mean DSC of 0.94 (95% CI, 0.93–0.95) in five-fold cross-validation on 106 examinations with manual reference segmentations. Iterative optimization progressively reduced manual processing time from approximately 10 hours of fully manual segmentation to less than 10 minutes of manual correction per patient. Application of the final model to the entire cohort enabled the generation of patient-specific three-dimensional reconstructions of the cranio-cervical venous system. The segmentation workflow was successfully integrated into the VNA software environment, allowing automated processing and visualization of MRI datasets. CONCLUSION This study demonstrates the feasibility of automated segmentation of the cranio-cervical venous system from contrast-enhanced MRI using a dedicated deep-learning pipeline. The resulting reduction in processing time and integration into an open-source software platform provide a foundation for future large-scale anatomical studies of cranio-cervical venous drainage. Summary Statement An automated nnU-Net-based MRI pipeline enabled segmentation and three-dimensional visualization of the cranio-cervical venous system, reducing manual correction time less than 10 minutes per case. Key Points - A dedicated nnU-Net v2-based pipeline was developed for MRI-based segmentation of the cranio-cervical venous system - Iterative model optimization reduced manual processing time from approximately 10 hours to less than 10 minutes per case. - The pipeline enabled patient-specific three-dimensional reconstructions and was integrated into a dedicated software environment for visualization and analyzis.

title: MLX-Radiomics: accelerating standardized regional and voxel-wise radiomics for CT, PET and MRI
abstract: BackgroundDifferences among radiomics implementations complicate cross-study comparisons, while voxel-wise feature extraction remains computationally demanding. We developed MLX-Radiomics to accelerate regional feature extraction and voxel-wise mapping while preserving agreement with standardized reference measurements. MethodsMLX-Radiomics implements 172 feature definitions from the Image Biomarker Standardization Initiative (IBSI), 16 extensions and the IBSI 2 image filters. We assessed agreement with IBSI reference data and evaluated numerical accuracy against independent double-precision and analytic calculations. In matched comparisons on Apple M1 Max and M5 Max systems, we used the IBSI reference CT to compare feature values, extraction time and memory use with PyRadiomics, MIRP and Flash-Radiomics, and feature values with FastRad. Separately, we compared the time required to generate voxel-wise feature maps for regions of up to 10.1 million voxels with published GPU results obtained on different hardware and images. We evaluated agreement with MIRP under published settings in a 51-patient cohort with CT, FDG PET and T1-weighted MRI. ResultsMLX-Radiomics agreed with all 2,160 IBSI reference measurements within the specified tolerances. With matching outputs, MLX-Radiomics was 2.66 to 7.27 times faster than PyRadiomics and MIRP for regional feature extraction and 198 to 218 times faster than PyRadiomics for voxel-wise mapping on a 243-voxel crop. It also outperformed the fastest Flash-Radiomics CPU configurations tested. On the M5 Max, generating 93 maps over 10.1 million voxels took 23.8 s. In the patient cohort, MLX-Radiomics and MIRP agreed on 98.0% of requested values. For tumors at the image edge, matching the libraries resampling rules substantially improved agreement. ConclusionsMLX-Radiomics provides standardized regional measurements and voxel-wise maps for CT, PET and MRI, with evidence of faster extraction limited to CT. It can support quantitative imaging research on relatively inexpensive hardware without requiring a separate GPU workstation.

title: OmniT2I: a unified table-to-image framework for survival prediction and cross-modal inference with incomplete multimodal cancer data
abstract: Molecular profiles and histopathology provide complementary information about cancer prognosis, but these data are often incomplete for individual patients. Here we present OmniT2I, a table-to-image framework for survival prediction and cross-modal inference from incomplete multimodal cancer data. Each molecular profile was converted into a three-channel image representation with correlation-based feature placement. OmniT2I combines available molecular and histopathology embeddings through availability-aware fusion and predicts missing modalities from those observed. Across 10,373 patients with 32 cancer types, the C-index was 0.631 within cancer types and 0.783 with all cancers pooled (0.660 and 0.787 in 5,605 patients with all five modalities). A single model handled all 31 modality combinations and, compared with nine survival methods trained separately for each, achieved higher C-indices in 240 of 279 pooled and 226 of 279 within-cancer comparisons. Adding predictions of withheld modalities to observed inputs improved pooled C-indices in all 180 pairings of observed and withheld modality sets and within-cancer C-indices in 164. Adding measured histopathology to RNA produced the largest within-cancer C-index gain among the four additional modalities evaluated, whereas adding copy number variation reduced it. In seven external cohorts, frozen RNA-only C-indices differed from test performance in the corresponding cancer type in TCGA by a median of −0.003 (range, −0.092 to +0.079). OmniT2I enables prognostic modeling with incomplete multimodal data.

title: WALRUS: Robust and Transferable Deep Learning for Water and Lipid Removal in 1H-MRSI
abstract: Proton magnetic resonance spectroscopic imaging (1H-MRSI) enables non-invasive mapping of brain metabolism, but reliable quantification is challenged by residual water and extracranial lipid contamination. Recent work demonstrated that a deep learning model trained on simulated metabolite spectra combined with in vivo-derived water and lipid signals can outperform conventional nuisance-removal methods. However, this approach relied on heuristic simulation parameter distributions and a subject-specific L2-derived lipid estimate as an auxiliary network input, requiring subject-specific lipid masks and L2 processing during inference. Here, we introduce WALRUS (Water And Lipid Removal Using Spectral Learning), a fitting-consistent and empirically calibrated framework developed through a systematic evaluation of simulation realism, architectural priors, and network optimization. WALRUS uses the same metabolite basis as downstream spectral fitting and calibrates deliberately broadened simulation distributions from in vivo measurements. Controlled 7 T experiments demonstrate that empirical simulator calibration substantially improves nuisance removal and metabolite quantification compared with heuristic training distributions. With the optimized simulator, a capacity-matched comparison reveals no clear additional benefit from the L2-derived prior, allowing its removal and substantially simplifying inference. Further improvements are achieved with the final higher-capacity U-Net, while on-the-fly simulation improves generalization compared with training on a fixed synthetic dataset. The same framework was subsequently recalibrated and retrained at 3 T, where WALRUS outperformed conventional HLSVD+L2 processing on held-out data. Together, WALRUS combines these advances into an optimized framework that improves nuisance removal and downstream metabolite fitting, requires no subject-specific lipid segmentation or L2-derived auxiliary input during inference, and can be systematically adapted to different acquisition settings.

title: Large Language Models to Label CT Radiology Reports for Incidental Findings Found in Lung Cancer Screening: A Comparative Analysis
abstract: ObjectiveTo compare LLM and prompting strategies for labeling Specific Incidental Findings (SIFs) occurring during lung cancer screening, in radiology reports. Materials and MethodsIn this retrospective study, 300 CT reports from a Dutch academic hospital were included between 19th March 2003 and 28th December 2020. GPT-5, GPT-4-Turbo, Llama-3.1-8B-INST, MedGemma-4B-IT, a keyword-based search method, and a radiologist labelled the reports for the presence or absence of nine SIFs. The radiologists scores were the reference standard. Each LLM was evaluated with four different prompting strategies: two without Chain-of-Thought (CoT), and two with CoT (one zero shot, one few shot). The automated labelling methods were evaluated against the radiologist primarily using Cohens Kappa, and additionally sensitivity, specificity, and F1 scores. ResultsGPT-5 achieved substantial or almost perfect agreement for seven out of nine SIFs: aortic valve disease, bronchiectasis, consolidation, coronary artery calcification, emphysema, abnormality in mediastinal lymph nodes, and thyroid abnormalities, with Cohen {kappa} values of 0.81 (0.70, 0.93), 0.97 (0.93, 1.00), 0.71 (0.62, 0.82), 0.92 (0.87, 0.96), 0.91 (0.84, 0.97), 0.71 (0.62, 0.80), and 0.92 (0.86, 0.98) respectively. For the remaining two SIFs, moderate LLM agreement was obtained with MedGemma-4B-IT and with GPT-4-Turbo with Cohen {kappa} values of 0.48 (0.40, 0.60), 0.42 (0.31, 0.58) for interstitial lung abnormalities and mediastinal mass respectively. The highest agreement was obtained with the non-CoT prompt strategies for most SIFs. ConclusionThis study demonstrated that LLMs can automatically label radiology reports with agreement ranging from almost perfect to moderate, but not one LLM - prompt combination achieved the highest agreement across all SIFs.

title: Cortical brain changes from early to mid-adolescence in offspring at familial high risk for schizophrenia or bipolar disorder
abstract: Objective: Schizophrenia (SZ) and bipolar disorder (BP) emerge in late adolescence or adulthood. Offspring at familial high risk for SZ (FHR-SZ) or BP (FHR-BP) are more likely to develop psychiatric disorders. Prior work from the Danish High Risk and Resilience (VIA) Study found sex-specific volumetric brain differences in offspring at FHR-SZ and FHR-BP aged 11-12 years. This study builds upon these findings by testing whether they reflect group differences in rate of change or stable group differences from early to mid-adolescence. Methods: This study investigated MRI data from offspring at FHR-SZ, FHR-BP, and population- based controls (PBC) at baseline (11-12 years; n=288) and follow-up (15-16 years; n=249). FreeSurfer longitudinal processing derived total brain volume, cortical measures, and intracranial volume (ICV). Linear mixed-effects models tested group-by-age interactions and sex-specific group effects, as well as associations with psychotic experiences (PE) and lifetime Axis-I mental disorders. Results: The analysis did not detect group-by-age interactions, indicating similar developmental slopes across groups. However, at both time points, males at FHR-SZ demonstrated reduced brain and cortical volumes compared to PBC and FHR-BP males. These effects were attenuated after adjusting for ICV, which was reduced in males at FHR-SZ. The analysis additionally detected volumetric reductions in males with PE, after controlling for risk status. Conclusions: These results extend the previous findings to ages 15-16 years, indicating group differences are stable and persist into mid-adolescence. Associations with ICV suggest early neurodevelopmental effects, and volumetric reductions in males with PE suggest convergent effects with FHR-SZ.

title: Lamina Cribrosa Strain as a Glaucoma Prognostic Factor: The STRAIN Study Methodology and Initial Outcomes
abstract: Objective To estimate the lamina cribrosa (LC) strain response to intraocular pressure (IOP) change in open angle glaucoma (OAG) patients and examine associations between LC strain and demographic and clinical characteristics relevant to OAG in an ongoing longitudinal study. Design Cohort study Participants Adult patients with OAG (205 eyes of 119 patients) Methods The STRAIN study is an ongoing longitudinal study designed to determine whether LC biomechanical strain is associated with present, prior, and future OAG damage. In this initial analysis, patients either temporarily stopped ≥1 eye drop, initiated an eye drop, or underwent selective laser trabeculoplasty to produce IOP change. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) scans of the optic nerve head (ONH) acquired before and up to several weeks after IOP change were analyzed using digital volume correlation (DVC) to estimate LC strain. Strain measurements were compared with age, race, sex, axial length, central corneal thickness (CCT), corneal hysteresis, optic disc area, years of known OAG, retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) thickness, and visual field mean deviation (MD). Main Outcome Measures LC strain estimated by DVC from OCT scans acquired before and after IOP alteration. Results Axial LC strain ( Ezz ) was tensile with IOP decrease and compressive with IOP increase. Maximum principal strain was tensile (mean E max = 1.09%), and maximum shear strain was positive (mean Γ max = 1.16%) in the radial-axial plane. Both increased quadratically with the IOP change. Older age was significantly related to greater tensile circumferential strain ( p = 0.02) and lower Γ max ( p = 0.01). Sex, CCT, corneal hysteresis, and optic disc area were not significantly associated with LC strain. In combined multivariable models adjusting for IOP change, demographics, and accounting for correlations between eyes from the same patient, eyes with thinner inferior-quadrant RNFL had smaller Γ max for a given IOP change ( p = 0.02). Conclusions LC strain in patients with OAG is associated with the degree of neuronal loss, age, and axial length, supporting a relationship between the LC biomechanical response and factors relevant to glaucomatous damage.

title: LungAI: An AI Biomarker that Refines Lung-RADS v2022 Triage of Screen-Detected Pulmonary Nodules
abstract: BackgroundThe Lung-RADS algorithm standardizes the management of screen-detected pulmonary nodules, but its risk assessment is driven chiefly by nodule size and attenuation. This misallocates a meaningful fraction of patients: a nontrivial share of small malignancies receive 12-month surveillance while large benign nodules proceed to invasive workup. Artificial intelligence (AI) may supply risk information independent of the imaging features Lung-RADS already uses. MethodsWe validated LungAI, an investigational deep learning nodule malignancy classifier not yet cleared by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), on the held-out NLST test partition of Ardila et al. (2,747 low-dose CT examinations from 1,244 patients with [≥]1 solid or part-solid 4-30 mm nodule; 89 pathologically confirmed cancers, prevalence 3.2%). We compared discrimination against Sybil, mean nodule diameter, and estimated nodule volume. A board-certified radiologist assigned Lung-RADS v2022 categories to a positives-enriched random subset (226 eligible examinations; 78 cancers), projected to the full cohort by contingency weighting. title: Beyond organ age gaps: comparing plasma proteomic metrics of organ biology in relation to brain structure and neurodegenerative disease
abstract: Biological aging is heterogeneous across organ systems, and brain health may be influenced by biological processes extending beyond the central nervous system (CNS). This can be investigated using biological age measures that are increasingly used to estimate how biological systems deviate from chronological aging. However, organ level plasma proteomic metrics may capture different forms of biological variation depending on how they are defined. Here, we compared three complementary organ level proteomic metrics across 15 organ systems (and two global systems) in relation to age, organ-relevant physiological phenotypes, brain morphometry, and incident neurodegenerative disease, using plasma proteomics from 52,667 UK Biobank participants and brain MRI data from 5,078 of those individuals. We derived i) supervised age gap metrics using XGBoost models trained to predict chronological age, ii) unsupervised PC1 metrics capturing dominant organ-associated proteomic variation, and iii) phenotype guided PLS metrics linking plasma proteins to organ-relevant physiological traits. The three metric classes were related but not interchangeable. Global all-protein and all-organ-protein models showed strong age-related proteomic structure. However, organ-specific PC analyses showed that age was often but not always the dominant source of variation in protein signal across organs. Age gap metrics showed the most consistent associations with subsequent ICD-10based neurodegenerative and vascular diagnoses, whereas all three metric classes showed distinct associations with brain structure and organ-relevant physiological phenotypes. Brain structure analyses revealed heterogeneous organ–brain association patterns across organs, suggesting that proteomic variation relates to brain structure in both a systemic and an organ-specific manner. Several systemic and organ-specific signals partially mediated the associations between disease specific genetic risk and incident diagnoses of Alzheimer’s disease and stroke, albeit with small effect sizes (1-8%). Similarly, organ metrics provided modest incremental predictive improvement over baseline demographic models, with the largest increase in ROC-AUC observed for Alzheimer’s disease when all organ age gap metrics were added jointly (ΔROC-AUC = 0.037). These results link brain related outcomes to proteomic variation across both CNS and non-CNS systems. Our work suggests that proteomic organ metrics capture complementary dimensions of biological variation rather than a single construct of organ aging. Although these measures may provide informative biological and potentially predictive signals, their incremental predictive value in the present analyses was modest.

title: Volumetric Analysis of the Deltoid Muscle From Neck-to-Knee Dixon MRI: A pilot population assessment of a posterior intramuscular injection target
abstract: BackgroundDeltoid muscle volume varies across anatomical regions and population groups, with potential implications for intramuscular injection site selection. Evidence comparing middle and posterior deltoid volumes in vaccine-eligible populations is limited. PurposeTo compare middle and posterior deltoid muscle volumes by vaccine eligibility group, sex, and side. MethodsDeltoid muscles were manually segmented into anterior, middle and posterior regions in 43 UK Biobank Dixon MRI scans. title: Silent Drift and Site-level Variance in Clinical AI: Real-world performance and subgroup analysis for post-market monitoring of an FDA-cleared artificial intelligence (AI) triage tool for high-risk use case of pulmonary embolism
abstract: BackgroundFDA-cleared artificial intelligence (AI) triage tool for pulmonary embolism (PE) detection has been widely used; however, its performance has not been analyzed for subgroups, clinical sites, and temporal stability. MethodsThis retrospective, six-site health system study evaluated the Aidoc BriefCase PE triage model (K190072) across 14,736 CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA) examinations between July 2023 and March 2026. Reference-standard PE characteristic labels were extracted from radiology reports using a zero-shot LLM pipeline validated against a radiologist-annotated 600 reports ({kappa} =0.98). Model performance was evaluated across demographics, embolus characteristics, and site. Temporal behavior was evaluated on operating point by logistic regression, with and without site adjustment, and by segmented regression. ResultsPE was present in 1,402/14,736 examinations (9.5%). Overall sensitivity was 64.1% (95% CI, 61.5-66.6%), specificity 98.8% (95% CI, 98.6-99.0%), compared with 93% sensitivity and 93.7% specificity in the FDA 510(k) summary. Sensitivity fell with peripherality (central 88.6%, lobar or segmental 63.1%, subsegmental 33.3%) and with chronicity (acute 65.5%, chronic 57.4%). Sensitivity differed significantly between the two highest-volume sites, 68.7% and 55.7% (P < .001), with CT scanner as the only variable different between the two sites. The false-positive rate fell 40% per year (P<.001) at a similar rate at two sites, while sensitivity fell 15% per year at site A (P<.036), from 72.5% to 65.0% between two halves of the study period. The manufacturer did not report model updates or threshold changes during the study period. ConclusionsDeployed sensitivity was substantially below the cleared benchmark and varied 13 points by site. The gradual shift in high specificity at the cost of low sensitivity, either from data drift or threshold change, either not monitored or not documented by the manufacturer, highlights the importance of independent continuous post-market monitoring.

title: Deep Learning Identifies BMI-Associated Morphologic Features in Breast Cancer Tissue
abstract: A bstract Multiple epidemiological studies have established obesity as an adverse factor in breast cancer incidence, progression, and clinical outcomes. However, the biological mechanisms underlying these associations remain incompletely understood. In peritumoral adipose tissue, obesity is associated with chronic inflammation, macrophage recruitment, and broader alterations in the local microenvironment. Whether these obesity-associated changes are accompanied by distinct morphologic features within the tumor and non-adipose stromal compartments remains unclear. In this study, we investigated whether an AI-based pathology foundation model could support the development of machine learning algorithms capable of identifying obesity-associated morphologic patterns in histopathology images, with a particular focus on tumor and stromal regions. In a cohort of 195 patients with breast cancer, machine learning models using vector embeddings from non-adipose stromal regions classified high BMI (≥30 kg/m 2 ) versus low BMI (<25 kg/m 2 ) with an average AUC of 0.78 (95% CI: 0.73–0.83), consistently outperforming models based on tumor-only or combined tumor–stroma regions. These obesity-associated stromal signatures were observed across subgroups defined by hormone-receptor status and age, indicating that they are not restricted to specific clinical populations. Complementary embedding-based dissimilarity analysis further showed that higher BMI was associated with reduced inter-patient heterogeneity in both tumor and stromal tissues. Overall, these findings suggest that obesity is associated with distinct morphologic alterations in both tumor and non-adipose stromal tissues. Notably, the stromal compartment emerged as a particularly informative indicator of obesity-associated morphology and demonstrated reduced inter-patient heterogeneity among individuals with high BMI.

title: A Multi-Cohort nnU-Net for White Matter Hyperintensity Segmentation Across 2D and 3D FLAIR Acquisitions
abstract: ABSTRACT Background White matter hyperintensities (WMH) are increasingly pooled across aging, cerebral small vessel disease (CSVD), and dementia cohorts that differ in both disease composition and FLAIR acquisition. Most automated segmentation tools were developed within a narrower range of populations or protocols, and few have been tested for whether segmentation accuracy and error remain consistent across conventional 2D and isotropic 3D FLAIR, or whether the choice of algorithm alters downstream clinical associations. Methods We developed a single nnU-Net model, taking FLAIR and T1-weighted images as inputs, using 460 2D and 3D FLAIR scans from a neurodegenerative cohort (Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, ADNI), a CSVD-enriched cohort with same-visit paired 2D and 3D FLAIR (Washington University White Matter Ischemic-Hypoxia study, WWISH), and a population-based sample (UK Biobank), holding out 92 scans from 66 participants at the participant-level as an internal test set. We further evaluated the model in an independent ADNI3 3D FLAIR set (n = 25), benchmarking voxel-wise overlap (Dice), volumetric agreement, and lesion-level detection against SHIVA-WMH, segcsvdWMH, and FreeSurfer WMH-SynthSeg, and compared acquisition-specific volume bias in participants with paired 2D and 3D FLAIR. We then compared how WMH volumes from each method predicted incident dementia in cognitively unimpaired adults from ADNI and the Knight Alzheimer Disease Research Center (n = 1,174; 42 incident cases). Results In the internal test set, the model achieved a mean Dice of 0.73 (SD 0.10), compared with 0.50, 0.57, and 0.29 for SHIVA-WMH, segcsvdWMH, and WMH-SynthSeg (all FDR-adjusted p < 0.001). Dice was similar on 2D and 3D FLAIR (0.75 vs. 0.71). In WWISH participants imaged with both acquisitions, mean volume bias differed between 2D and 3D scans by 1.8 mL for the model versus 4.7–9.9 mL for the comparators. Advantages were largest in low-burden scans (<5 mL; Dice 0.66 vs. 0.19–0.54) and for lesions of ≤100 voxels (detection 77–87% vs. 14–63%). In ADNI3, the model retained a mean Dice of 0.70 (SD 0.14) without retraining and exceeded all comparators (FDR-adjusted p ≤ 0.002). Model-derived WMH volume was associated with incident dementia beyond clinical covariates (OR per SD 1.40, 95% CI 1.11–1.77; likelihood-ratio p = 0.009; cross-validated AUC 0.71 vs. 0.68), whereas comparator-derived volumes did not significantly improve model fit. Conclusions Training a single model across disease contexts and FLAIR acquisitions yielded WMH segmentation that was similarly accurate on 2D and 3D FLAIR, sensitive to low-burden disease, transferable to an unseen protocol, and clinically informative, supporting its use in multi-cohort, mixed-etiology studies. Only WMH volume from the model significantly improved model fit for incident dementia beyond clinical covariates, highlighting the potential influence of segmentation algorithm choice on downstream clinical inference.

title: Reliability-Aware Clinical Relation Learning for Uncertainty-Robust Multi-Label Chest X-ray Classification
abstract: Background Automated multi-label classification of chest radiographs is complicated by overlapping imaging findings, noisy report-derived labels, and changes in disease co-occurrence across clinical settings. Existing clinical-hierarchy methods can encode label relationships, but a rigid hierarchy may conflate categorical membership with empirical association and propagate annotation errors. Methods We investigated Reliability-Aware Clinical Relation Learning (ReCaRL), a graph-assisted framework for multi-label chest radiograph classification. An image encoder produces initial finding scores, while a graph constructed from training-label associations provides reliability-weighted, confidence-gated updates. Uncertain annotations are handled with observation masks. The evaluation compares flat, weighted, graph-based, and hierarchy-penalty baselines, with internal and external discrimination and calibration assessments. Results In the internal evaluation, ReCaRL achieved macro AUROC 0.821 and macro AUPRC 0.437, compared with 0.812 and 0.423 for the masked/weighted baseline. Mean AUROC across five common findings was 0.865 versus 0.858. External testing yielded AUROC 0.799 and AUPRC 0.409. Post-hoc calibration reduced the internal Brier score from 0.113 to 0.102 and the external expected calibration error from 0.082 to 0.061, without changing AUROC or AUPRC. Conclusions Reliability-aware graph propagation and confidence gating were associated with modest improvements in multi-label chest radiograph classification relative to the matched masked/weighted baseline. Post-hoc calibration improved probability reliability in the reported evaluations. The findings do not establish a benefit in prospective clinical decision-making.

abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-based computer-aided detection (CAD) of tuberculosis (TB) on chest X-ray (CXR) may standardize screening and triage in settings with few radiologists but its accuracy in clinical cohorts remains uncertain. title: Circular-Arc Modal Migration for Ultrasound Imaging—Part I: Finite-Arc Spectral Theory and Stolt–Pullback Factorization
abstract: Circular-arc ultrasound imaging requires a spectral construction that accommodates radius-dependent propagation and the spatially varying phase of offset-source transmission. This first of two articles develops Circular-Arc Modal Migration (CAMM), a direct Stolt-type imaging framework in angular modal coordinates. Starting from a first-Born acoustic model, angular decomposition and local radial Stolt mappings convert channel spectra into fields for coherent image synthesis. The offset transmit phase is represented by a phase-screen factorization through reusable spectral factors and spatially weighted fields. A scalar-pullback approximation simplifies this correction to reading one reference image at a geometrically fitted radial coordinate. Both realizations share the same modal construction. Error controls address local radial synthesis, transmit-path expansion, scalar approximation, and phase-screen truncation, with direct integration verifying the separated numerical evaluation. Same-RF point-target comparisons show that scalar pullback closely preserves the principal peak positions and widths of phase-screen imaging in the compact semicircular configuration, while phase screens better control surrounding responses in the shallow convex examples. The retained modal spectrum, frequency band, image radius, and source displacement guide this accuracy–computation choice. CAMM thereby extends direct spectral image formation to circular arcs and supplies the theoretical and numerical basis for the image-quality and performance studies in Part II.

title: Anatomy-preserving rare-subregion correction for pediatric brain tumor segmentation on multiparametric MRI: a BraTS-PEDs 2026 challenge study
abstract: Pediatric brain tumor subregion segmentation is strongly imbalanced: whole-tumor anatomy is comparatively stable, whereas enhancing tumor (ET), cystic component (CC), and edema (ED) may be absent or small. We present an anatomy-preserving multi-stage system for BraTS-PEDs 2026 Task 2. A five-fold residual-encoder nnU-Net supplies robust anatomy and calibrated out-of-fold priors. Candidate ET and CC regions are recovered by independent fold agreement and component-level filters. A rare-aware residual adapter then operates only inside voxels labeled non-enhancing tumor core (NETC), using MRI, signed intermodality contrasts, probability uncertainty, spatial anatomy, and coordinates. Its constrained assembly permits only NETC-to-ET or NETC-to-CC transitions; therefore background, ED, tumor core, and whole tumor are invariant. On 236 out-of-fold cases, the adapter improved CC Dice from 0.223 to 0.253 and CC normalized surface Dice from 0.233 to 0.263, while preserving tumor-core and whole-tumor scores exactly. The frozen Docker submission achieved Dice scores of 0.510, 0.908, 0.144, 0.000, 0.937, and 0.937 for ET, NETC, CC, ED, tumor core, and whole tumor, respectively, on the 91-case challenge validation set. The results show that constrained rare-subtype correction can improve difficult labels without sacrificing strong anatomical predictions, while also exposing persistent domain shift for CC and ED.

title: TRACE: Trajectory Reconstruction and Clustering from Sparse Evidence for Disease Subtyping and Staging
abstract: A bstract Chronic progressive diseases often follow heterogeneous courses, with individuals differing in the pattern and timing of biomarker abnormalities. However, observed data are typically sparse and predominantly cross-sectional, with limited follow-up covering only short segments of disease progression. Reconstructing heterogeneous trajectories from such data requires disentangling variation along disease trajectories from subtype heterogeneity while inferring individuals’ unknown sub-type assignments and disease stages. Existing approaches may confound disease stage with subtype, scale poorly as the number of biomarkers increases, or fail to effectively integrate cross-sectional and longitudinal observations. We propose TRACE ( T rajectory R econstruction A nd C lustering from Sparse E vidence), a probabilistic framework that jointly reconstructs biomarker trajectories and infers disease subtypes and continuous stages. TRACE combines monotonic neural networks for flexible modeling and data-driven clustering of subtype-specific progression trajectories with temporal regularization derived from longitudinal observations when available. All model components are jointly optimized end to end using stochastic gradient descent, enabling efficient and scalable estimation. We evaluate TRACE on semi-simulated MRI biomarker data with known subtype and stage structures and demonstrate its ability to identify clinically meaningful subtypes and disease stages in real-world neurodegenerative disease datasets.

title: Anatomy-Aware 3D GAN with Local Mask Refinement for Brain MRI Inpainting
abstract: Brain tumor MRI inpainting aims to synthesize plausible healthy-appearing tissue in regions removed from pathological scans. We present an anatomy-aware three-dimensional generative adversarial network for Task 4 of the BraTS 2026 challenge. The method combines mask-aware gated convolutions, mirrored contralateral context, attention-modulated skip fusion, boundary-aware refinement, and a local masked-region refiner, each adapted from established components in the image synthesis and inpainting literature. The model is trained with a two-stage objective that first emphasizes voxel-wise and structural reconstruction and then applies low-weight adversarial fine-tuning. On a deterministic local held-out split, the proposed method substantially improves over a simple 3D AutoEncoder baseline but does not surpass the challenge's Pix2Pix3D baseline. On the official BraTS 2026 Task 4 evaluation server, the submitted model obtained a mean SSIM of 0.658 and a mean PSNR of 14.81~dB over 219 evaluated cases, lower than the local held-out figures. We report these results transparently, analyze likely contributing factors, and identify the controlled ablations (removal of the mirrored-context channel and of the two-stage schedule) required to isolate the contribution of each architectural component.

title: Deep-learning body composition analysis of routine CT robust to scan range, slice order and contrast phase
abstract: Purpose: To develop and validate a fully automated pipeline that measures skeletal muscle and adipose tissue at L1 and L3 on routine CT with varied scan ranges, slice orders and contrast phases, rejects levels outside the scan and converts measures to non-contrast equivalents. Materials and methods: The pipeline (sarco) combines orientation detection, L1/L3 localisation with out-of-range rejection, U-Net segmentation, six-class contrast-phase estimation, phase-specific conversion to non-contrast-equivalent values and, as an auxiliary output, muscle and marrow age estimation. We evaluated it on five single-centre datasets (4986 series): agreement with radiologist-corrected labels using five-fold cross-fitting (2025 series), artificially truncated scans, contrast-enhanced series paired with non-contrast series of the same examination, and the prognostic value of fully automated measures in 2006 patients after curative cancer surgery. TotalSegmentator served as a comparator. Results: On held-out folds, L3 skeletal muscle area (SMA) agreed with the reference (intraclass correlation coefficient 0.983; bias +1.35 cm2). On truncated scans processed with cross-fitted localisation models, the chosen L3 slice was off by half a vertebra or more in 4.7-5.6% of volumes (TotalSegmentator 11.3-14.3%). Four-group phase accuracy was 0.949, exceeding TotalSegmentator in scans shorter than 400 mm (0.952-0.960 vs 0.643-0.668), and conversion reduced the root mean square error of L3 muscle attenuation against the same-examination non-contrast series from 7.96 to 2.81 HU. Combined age estimates had a mean absolute error of 6.5 years. Automatically measured low muscle mass increased the cross-validated Uno's C of the baseline model by 0.034 (95% CI 0.009-0.053; cancer-specific survival) and 0.031 (0.016-0.048; overall survival), whereas converted L3 muscle attenuation added 0.012 (-0.005 to 0.024) for overall survival. Conclusion: The pipeline provides robust, contrast-phase-aware body composition measures from routine CT with varied scan ranges and reproduces known prognostic associations without manual input.

title: Segment Anything for Microscopy 2
abstract: Foundation models have advanced microscopy image segmentation, but existing models are trained on two-dimensional data, struggle with complex structures in volumetric data, and address only a narrow range of analysis tasks. Here we present Segment Anything for Microscopy 2 (μSAM2), a foundation model that adapts SAM2 to joint 2D and 3D segmentation in light and electron microscopy. Trained on annotations of more than 23 million cells and nuclei and 1.6 million cellular structures, μSAM2 achieves state-of-the-art automatic and interactive segmentation and outperforms generalist and specialist methods on volumetric data. Dedicated models further enable accurate mitochondrion and nucleus segmentation in electron microscopy. Beyond segmentation, μSAM2 supports pixel and object classification from few annotations as well as cell tracking in 2D and 3D time-lapse data. All functionality is available in the user-friendly μSAM napari plugin. We demonstrated the capabilities of μSAM2 on challenging use cases spanning developmental biology, organoid research, cardiac physiology, and histopathology.

title: Restoring Marcenko-Pastur noise estimation and denoising of diffusion MRI under common image reconstruction
abstract: Diffusion magnetic resonance imaging can reveal microstructure in the living brain, but the measurements are inherently noisy. Marcenko-Pastur denoising is a widely used remedy, helping to separate signal from noise under a simplified noise covariance model. However, we find that the model breaks under common image reconstructions across 28 public in vivo datasets, resulting in weaker denoising than intended. We restore the intended denoising behavior with a noise covariance model estimated from the reconstructed images, and validate the estimated model on repeated ex vivo and in vivo scans. The method requires no additional measurements or knowledge of the reconstruction, opening headroom for microstructure analyses in both existing and newly acquired data.

title: Cortical surface area is an independent predictor of incident dementia
abstract: Cortical surface area (cSA) is associated with intelligence and cognition, yet structural MRI studies of neurodegeneration in Alzheimers disease and related dementias (ADRD) have emphasized quantification of cortical thickness (cTH) and volume, with very limited evaluation of cSA. We examined whether cSA of AD-relevant brain regions provide diagnostic, prognostic, and biological information beyond cTH and volume across 5,430 participants (3,124 cognitively unimpaired; 1,634 mild cognitive impairment [MCI]; 672 ADRD) from three aging and dementia cohorts: the National Alzheimers Coordinating Center, Alzheimers Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, and Carotids and Minds study. In cross-sectional analyses, cSA and cTH showed weak correlation, and lower cSA was independently associated with greater odds of MCI and ADRD after adjustment for cTH and covariates. Participants with both low cSA and low cTH had greater risk of MCI and ADRD compared to low cSA, cTH, or volume alone. In longitudinal models, baseline cSA predicted incident ADRD independent from cTH, and combined cSA/cTH models outperformed cSA, cTH, or volume alone for predicting incident ADRD over a mean follow-up of 4.3 years. Complementing these findings, proteomics analyses revealed distinct signatures associated with cSA compared to cTH. Overall, these findings support cSA as a clinically informative and biologically distinct dimension of AD-related cortical vulnerability.

title: MeXalign - A Segmentation Mask-Based Registration Pipeline for Multimodal Single-Cell Analysis
abstract: Leveraging the power of multimodal imaging relies on accurate coregistration of yet fundamentally different modalities. Reliable cell-to-cell correspondence is especially challenging as consecutive tissue sections do not necessarily contain identical cells or cellular structures. Here we present MeXalign, a segmentation-mask-based coregistration pipeline designed to integrate multimodal images acquired sequentially from the same specimen at single-cell resolution. Single-cell segmentation masks provide a modality-independent representation of cellular morphology and spatial organization. MeXalign was tested based on the two platforms, laser ablation inductively coupled plasma time-of-flight mass spectrometry (LA-ICP-TOFMS) and immunofluorescence (IF) microscopy. As a prerequisite, each modality integrates membrane and/or nucleus labels for accurate segmentation. The added value of MeXalign was highlighted for imaging of cell models deposited on glass slides and tissue sections. The performance of coregistration was validated on cytospins, murine tumor and human skin samples. A dedicated scoring system was introduced allowing to assess the quality of image coregistration. The robustness towards under-segmentation and downstream image analysis was evaluated on LA-ICP-TOFMS with and without coregistration, investigating metal drug uptake, barcoding and cellular phenotyping. A showcase study on cancer cells exposed to nanoparticles proved the accuracy, as the nanoparticle distribution was preserved at a subcellular level when using MeXalign. While all examples show the overall improved quality of segmentation, other benefits of complementary labelings can be anticipated, especially for cellular features unique to one modality.

title: MR-based normative volumetric analyses reveal genotype-dependent brain anomalies in FGFR-related craniosynostoses
abstract: Craniostenosis, a cranial malformation due to premature suture fusion, includes rare FGFR related conditions such as Crouzon (CS), Muenke (MS), and Apert (AS) syndromes. These mutations affect skull but also brain development and are associated with variable neurodevelopmental outcomes. This brain impairment is still poorly described and understood, prompting for neuroimaging anatomical studies. We thus investigated regional brain growth and volumetric scaling in patients with these three syndromes and non-syndromic non FGFR related craniostenoses, using a normative modelling framework. We analyzed a rare set of brain MRI from 65 patients close to first cranial surgery time (30 CS among which 23 pre-surgery, 4 AS, 6 MS, 23 non syndromic) and 130 typically developing controls. Millimetric 3D T1 weighted images were segmented into 6 cortical and 3 subcortical regions (AssemblyNet, Morphologist). After harmonization (ComBat), normative growth curves (Turner model) and static scaling curves (power law model, effect of brain size regardless of age) were derived in controls. Patient deviations were assessed using permutation tests on mean normalized distance to typical model and abnormality rates (10th/90th percentiles). Patients with CS showed typical brain volumes for age except for enlarged ventricles, but slightly overscaled frontal volumes for brain size. Non-syndromic patients showed very similar volume distribution for age and brain size than CS ones. Patients with AS displayed increased total brain, temporal, cerebellar and central volumes for age, with overscaled temporal and cerebellar regions but underscaled frontal volumes for brain size. Patients with MS showed a similar, though milder, pattern: increased temporal volume for age, with temporal overscaling but frontal underscaling for frain size. Our findings reveal genotype dependent brain anomalies in FGFR related craniosynostoses, with a convergent pattern of temporal frontal disproportions in AS and MS, associated with very specific mutations in the FGFR2 and 3 genes respectively, contrasting with a much more typical brain organization in more heterogeneous CS and non syndromic patients. Beyond the pathophysiological meaning of these results, which call for a larger similar study covering as wide a range of patient variability as possible, our work highlights the relevance of normative modelling approach for characterizing rare craniofacial disorders using clinical MRI datasets.

title: Normative Modeling of Structural and Diffusion MRI for Epilepsy Diagnosis and Classification
abstract: Background: and Objectives: Normative modeling expresses an individual's brain measures as deviations from a large healthy reference and has been advanced as a route to precision imaging biomarkers in epilepsy, where structural abnormality is distributed rather than confined to the presumed focus. Whether this framework can inform clinical classification from clinically acquired T1-weighted and diffusion MRI is untested. We asked whether normative deviations discriminate between (1) epilepsy and functional seizures; (2) focal and generalized epilepsy; and (3) drug-resistant and drug-responsive epilepsy. Methods: We retrospectively studied patients with epilepsy or functional seizures without comorbid epilepsy who underwent 3-Tesla epilepsy-protocol MRI at the University of Pennsylvania. Morphometric deviation scores (cortical thickness, subcortical volume) were derived from CentileBrain (n>37,000 healthy references). White matter fractional anisotropy and mean diffusivity profiles were referenced to harmonized Human Connectome Project cohorts. Lobar composites, hemispheric asymmetry indices, and whole-tract means were compared with rank-sum tests; discrimination was summarized as area under the ROC curve (AUC) with bootstrap confidence intervals and Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Whole-brain deviation burden was examined as a secondary analysis. Minimum detectable effects were estimated by Monte Carlo simulation at 80% power (α=0.05). Results: We included 273 patients with epilepsy (203 focal, 37 generalized, 33 unclassified; 97 drug-resistant, 176 drug-responsive) and 32 with functional seizures. In the primary analyses, no regional or tract-level normative measure distinguished epilepsy from functional seizures, focal from generalized epilepsy, or drug-resistant from drug-responsive epilepsy; AUCs did not exceed 0.62, with upper confidence limits up to 0.72. In the secondary analysis, whole-brain morphometric deviation burden was modestly higher in epilepsy than in functional seizures (AUC 0.66, 95% CI 0.57-0.74) but did not separate the within-epilepsy comparisons. The study could detect AUC ≥0.65 for epilepsy versus functional seizures, ≥0.64 for focal versus generalized, and ≥0.60 for drug-resistant versus drug-responsive epilepsy. Discussion: Univariate normative deviation summaries from clinical MRI do not currently distinguish these groups well enough to guide care. Whole-brain deviation burden, the only summary measure that differed after correction, was detectable at the group level but insufficient for individual-level classification. Progress may require network-targeted analysis of patient-specific deviations and multimodal integration.

title: Integrating Histopathology Foundation Models and PRAME Immunohistochemistry in Melanoma Diagnosis
abstract: Background: The histopathological diagnosis of challenging melanocytic lesions remains limited by substantial interobserver variability. Although computational pathology foundation models demonstrated promising diagnostic performance, their predictions are often difficult to interpret in terms of established criteria. Objective: We evaluated a diagnostic framework combining foundation-model-based whole-slide image analysis, automated prediction of morphological features, and manually assessed PRAME immunohistochemistry. Methods: Using the Virchow2 foundation model and STAMP framework, we analyzed a retrospective cohort of 1,000 melanocytic lesions undergoing PRAME immunohistochemistry. Models were trained on 800 cases and evaluated on a temporally held-out test cohort of 200 cases. Results: The slide-level malignancy classifier achieved a test AUROC of 0.970 (AUPRC 0.984). Separate models predicted established histopathological criteria with high discrimination, including ulceration (AUROC 0.991) and dermal mitoses (AUROC 0.966). In contrast, predicting PRAME expression from H&E images alone showed lower performance (AUROC 0.776-0.780 for PRAME scores 4 and 0). An integrated model combining the slide-level malignancy score, AI-predicted morphological features, and manual PRAME status achieved an AUROC of 0.972 (AUPRC 0.975), comparable to the standalone classifier. In multivariable analysis, PRAME score 4 versus 0 was strongly associated with malignancy (adjusted OR 35.04, 95% CI 17.39-74.62). Conclusions: These findings demonstrate the feasibility of combining foundation-model-based histopathological analysis with established morphological criteria and PRAME immunohistochemistry. Although the integrated framework did not substantially improve overall discrimination, it provides a structured approach for incorporating complementary histopathological and immunohistochemical information into AI-assisted assessment of melanocytic lesions.

title: Deep learning of point-of-care lung ultrasound and clinical data for pulmonary tuberculosis triage in Uganda
abstract: Rationale: Point of care lung ultrasound is portable and radiation free and could extend tuberculosis screening to settings without chest radiography, but no standardized criteria exist for interpreting it for tuberculosis. Objectives: To develop and internally evaluate deep learning models that classify pulmonary tuberculosis from lung ultrasound images, alone and combined with routine clinical variables, and to derive an abbreviated scanning protocol. Methods: In a prospective study in Kampala, Uganda (2023 to 2025), we enrolled people aged 13 years or older with microbiologically confirmed pulmonary tuberculosis, their household contacts, and symptomatic people with other respiratory conditions. One still frame from each of 12 lung ultrasound zones was analyzed with an attention-based multiple-instance learning network. We compared clinical-only (random forest), ultrasound only, and combined models and derived a 6 zone protocol from training set attention weights. Participants were allocated to training (n = 223), validation (n = 20), and held-out test (n = 73) sets. Results: Of 318 enrolled participants, 316 were analyzed (118 with and 198 without tuberculosis). In the test set, areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve were 0.88 (95% confidence interval, 0.80 to 0.95) for the clinical-only model; 0.93 (0.86 to 0.97) and 0.95 (0.89 to 0.99) for the 12 zone ultrasound-only and combined models; and 0.91 (0.83 to 0.97) and 0.93 (0.86 to 0.99) for the corresponding 6-zone models. At 90% sensitivity, specificity was 82.2% (34.9 to 97.8) for the 12-zone combined model and 91.1% (25.0 to 98.0) for the 6-zone combined model. Point estimates for all 12-zone models and the 6-zone combined model met the 2025 World Health Organization minimum accuracy targets for a high-sensitivity screening test (≥90% sensitivity, ≥60% specificity). Conclusion: Lung ultrasound analyzed with attention-based deep learning and combined with clinical variables showed high internal discrimination for pulmonary tuberculosis, and a simplified 6-zone protocol retained most of this performance. External validation in intended-use screening populations is needed

title: Rapid screening of target-specific isotope labeling protocols for in situ NMR of bacterial membrane proteins
abstract: We describe an approach for the efficient development of targeted isotope labeling protocols leading to nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) structural studies of bacterial membrane proteins in intact cells and native outer membrane (OM) vesicles (OMVs). The assay relies on the bioorthogonal non-canonical amino acid tagging (BONCAT) approach for metabolic incorporation of an azide-bearing residue, followed by copper-catalyzed azide-alkyne cycloaddition (CuAAC) to an alkyne-functionalized fluorescent dye. Fluorescence detection in SDS-PAGE provides a rapid way to test samples for off-target background signal from endogenous proteins, bypassing the need for intensive NMR screening experiments. Using this approach, we develop an optimized protocol that enables high-resolution NMR spectra to be obtained in situ with negligible background signal. The BONCAT approach also enables target-specific fluorescence or nano-gold labeling of proteins at the OM surface, further extending the utility of this protocol for correlative structure-activity studies of membrane proteins in situ.

title: Age and Sex Differences in Lateral Ventricle Choroid Plexus Volume in a Large, Manually Segmented, Multi-Site MRI Dataset
abstract: Introduction: The choroid plexus (ChP), which produces cerebrospinal fluid and forms the blood-CSF barrier, has drawn growing interest in psychiatric and neurodegenerative neuroimaging. However, prior volumetric studies have relied largely on automated segmentation tools such as FreeSurfer, which show poor agreement with manual tracing, and have been limited to small, narrow-age, single-site samples. Methods We present DataPlex, a manually segmented lateral ventricle ChP dataset comprising 700 3T T1-weighted MRI scans drawn from 35 study/site categories, spanning a wide range of age, sex, and scanner manufacturer (GE, Philips, Siemens). Using generalized least squares models accounting for within-site dependence, we examined associations between ChP and lateral ventricle (LV) volume, and age, sex, scanner manufacturer, image resolution, a registration-based quality-control metric, intracranial volume, and cognitive performance. Results ChP volume displayed a positive linear association with age and was significantly greater in males than females, while LV volume showed a significant nonlinear relationship with age and no sex difference. Scanner manufacturer and image resolution were significantly associated with measured left LV volume but not with ChP volume, and the quality-control metric was not significantly associated with any outcome. Both ChP and LV volume were significantly associated with several cognitive domains, including emotion recognition, working memory, inhibitory control, and episodic memory. Conclusion These findings demonstrate meaningful differences in ChP volume across age and sex. DataPlex represents the largest demographically and technically diverse manually segmented ChP dataset to date, establishing reference benchmarks for future automated segmentation tools and underscoring the importance of accounting for demographic and technical covariates in choroid plexus research.

title: Automated segmentation of renal structures using brightfield images of unstained kidney biopsies
abstract: The automated segmentation of unstained kidney brightfield microscopy images remains a significant challenge in medical imaging. In conventional histopathology, staining provides crucial structural and molecular contrast, allowing renal compartments and structures to be readily distinguished. The absence of staining markedly reduces this contrast, obscuring the fine architectural details that are essential for diagnosis. Addressing this gap would reduce reliance on staining protocols, reduce technical and interpretive variability, and preserve valuable tissue for downstream molecular or multi-omics analyses. Ultimately, automation of unstained image segmentation could enable faster, more objective tissue analysis while preserving samples for further molecular testing. In this work, we provide a comprehensive review of state-of-the-art segmentation methods applied to renal brightfield microscopy images. Current findings highlight a predominance of Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) based architectures for semantic segmentation approaches while recent trends point to the growing application of transformer-based and instance-segmentation strategies. However, the field is still hampered by the scarcity and poor annotation of publicly available renal datasets. Aiming to further contribute to the enhancement of the field, a dataset of 18 Whole Slide Images (WSIs) of unstained human kidney tissue is made publicly available. Additionally, in the dataset, we provide 543 annotated tiles extracted from the WSIs, facilitating further research into stain-independent segmentation approaches. As a third contribution, we present a preliminary case study, evaluating state-of-the-art deep learning segmentation architectures, including U-Net and Segment Anything Model (SAM). Our preliminary results indicate that deep learning models demonstrate promising segmentation performance in unstained kidney biopsies. In alignment with these findings, advanced customised loss functions and data augmentation were integrated into the supervised training of the promising U-Net, DeepLabv3+, and TransUNet models, achieving significant improvements compared to the baseline experiments. To exploit the abundance of unlabelled data, we further tested FixMatchSeg, a semi-supervised learning method; however, its segmentation performance remained slightly behind the supervised methods. Taken together, these contributions establish a foundation for future research in stain-independent Computational Pathology, demonstrating that unstained brightfield microscopy images can reliably support downstream tissue analysis tasks. Our dataset, validation experiments, and methodological insights provide the community with both resources and benchmarks to advance robust, data-efficient, and generalisable kidney tissue segmentation.

title: Focused ultrasound-enhanced carboplatin delivery improves radiotherapy response and survival in a preclinical glioblastoma model
abstract: Rationale Glioblastoma is highly resistant to conventional therapies due to the limited penetration of chemotherapeutics across the blood-brain and blood-tumor barriers (BBB, BTB). Although platinum-based drugs show strong cytotoxic and radiosensitizing properties in several cancers, their inability to achieve therapeutic concentrations within the central nervous system (CNS) severely limits their efficacy in brain tumors. This study investigated whether focused ultrasound (FUS)-mediated BBB/BTB disruption combined with intravenous carboplatin and stereotactic radiotherapy could improve drug delivery, tumor control, and survival in a preclinical glioblastoma model. Methods F98 glioma-bearing rats were treated with a single dose of 15 Gy radiation therapy (RT), carboplatin only, carboplatin + RT, FUS + carboplatin or FUS + carboplatin + RT. FUS-mediated permeabilization was confirmed by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and platinum accumulation was quantified by inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry and synchrotron X-ray fluorescence. Tumor progression and microenvironmental changes were monitored using multiparametric MRI (diffusion, perfusion, and vascular permeability), followed by voxel-wise clustering analysis and histopathological validation. Results The FUS + carboplatin + RT group demonstrated the strongest therapeutic benefit, compared to all other treatment groups, yielding up to a 122% increase in median survival relative to the untreated group. This treatment also reduced necrotic core expansion and induced a transient increase in tumor perfusion, suggesting improved vascular function. FUS enhanced carboplatin delivery to both the tumor and peritumoral brain, with platinum distribution closely correlating with MRI signal enhancement. Voxel-wise clustering of multiparametric MRI identified biologically distinct tumor regions that were subsequently validated by immunohistochemistry. Conclusion The combination of FUS-mediated carboplatin delivery and radiotherapy represents a safe, non-invasive strategy that enhances drug delivery and improves survival in an aggressive preclinical model of glioblastoma. By overcoming a major limitation of current therapies, this approach shows promising potential for clinical translation. title: [MRI of suspected bone and soft tissue sarcomas - an overview].
abstract: Sarcomas are rare malignant tumors of connective and supportive tissues, associated with relatively poor five-year survival. According to Swedish patient care bundles ("standardiserat vårdförlopp"), MRI should be performed at local radiology departments before a possible referral to a sarcoma center when there is a strong suspicion of a soft tissue sarcoma, highlighting the need for adequate knowledge of appopriate MRI protocols. For soft tissue lesions, MRI is diagnostic only for a few entities, such as simple lipomas. Most muskuloskeletal tumors, however, require biopsy for definitive diagnosis. Consequently, MRI is primarily used to assess tumor extent prior to biopsy and potential surgery. The Swedish Society of Musculoskeletal Radiology (SFMSR) recommends that an MRI protocol for musculoskeletal tumors should always consist of at least the following three sequences: coronal STIR FSE, axial T1-weighted FSE, and axial T2-weighted FSE. Coronal STIR is mainly used for tumor detection and evaluation of lipomatous lesions. Axial T1 is primarily used to assess intraosseous tumor extent and characterize lipomatous lesions. Axial T2 is primarily used to evaluate soft tissue tumor extension and extraosseous components of bone tumors.

title: Presacral Myelolipoma Mimicking Liposarcoma Complicated by Massive Intraoperative Hemorrhage: A Case Report.
abstract: Introduction Myelolipoma is a benign tumor composed of mature adipose tissue and hematopoietic elements. Extra-adrenal lesions can occur in the presacral region and may mimic liposarcoma. Resection of a large presacral tumor can also cause life-threatening hemorrhage. We report a presacral myelolipoma that was difficult to diagnose preoperatively and was complicated by massive intraoperative hemorrhage. Case presentation A 71-year-old woman had an incidentally detected 75 × 75 × 125-mm presacral mass with mixed fatty and solid components on contrast-enhanced CT. MRI showed restricted diffusion, and fluorodeoxyglucose PET/CT showed mild uptake (maximum standardized uptake value, 3.93). No growth occurred over approximately 3 months. Because liposarcoma could not be excluded, the patient chose open resection without biopsy for diagnosis and treatment. During cranial dissection along the anterior sacrum, massive bleeding occurred from the right internal iliac venous system, and systolic blood pressure decreased to 50-60 mmHg. Manual compression was insufficient, and massive transfusion was initiated. Intraoperatively, a vein communicating with the right internal iliac vein was found to enter the tumor, and the main trunk of the right internal iliac vein was ligated near its junction with the right common iliac vein. Persistent bleeding required ligation of a tumor-entering branch of the right internal iliac artery; the arterial main trunk was preserved. Hemostasis was prioritized, and the tumor was removed in 2 pieces; the capsule was disrupted without macroscopic tumor spillage. Diffuse presacral venous plexus bleeding was controlled with electrocautery and oxidized cellulose. Operative time was 3 h 21 min, and blood loss was 4850 mL; 10 units of leukocyte-reduced red blood cells and 6 units of fresh frozen plasma were transfused. Histopathological examination established the diagnosis of myelolipoma. No vascular complications occurred, and contrast-enhanced CT at approximately 1 year showed no residual or recurrent tumor. Conclusions Presacral myelolipoma should be considered in the differential diagnosis of fat-containing presacral tumors. In large tumors, the relationship with the internal iliac vessels and presacral venous plexus should be carefully assessed, and adequate blood products, early vascular control, and source-specific hemostatic techniques should be prepared before resection.

title: Emergency Resection for Perforated Small Bowel Metastasis from Primary Lung Cancer During Systemic Therapy: A Case Report.
abstract: Introduction Small bowel metastases from lung cancer may remain clinically occult until serious complications, including obstruction, bleeding, and perforation, occur. We report a case of perforated jejunal metastasis with a synchronous ileal metastasis at high risk of obstruction, identified during emergency surgery while several previously documented extraintestinal lesions had decreased in size. Case presentation A 75-year-old woman with metastatic non-small cell lung carcinoma favoring adenocarcinoma had a programmed death-ligand 1 tumor proportion score of 95% and no targetable alteration on the companion-diagnostic panel. Pembrolizumab monotherapy (200 mg intravenously every 3 weeks) was administered for 4 cycles; no antiangiogenic agent had been administered concurrently or previously. Eleven days after the 4th dose, she developed acute abdominal pain. CT showed focal small bowel wall thickening, adjacent extraluminal air, diffuse bowel edema, and ascites. Emergency surgery revealed a perforated jejunal tumor approximately 20 cm distal to the ligament of Treitz. Systematic examination of the entire small bowel identified a 2nd, nearly circumferential ileal tumor approximately 15 cm proximal to the terminal ileum with marked luminal narrowing; both lesions were resected. Histopathological examination showed metastatic poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma of pulmonary origin. Neither tumor necrosis nor a histological treatment effect was identified, and the non-neoplastic mucosa showed no findings suggestive of immune checkpoint inhibitor-related enteritis. The patient was discharged on POD 19. Pembrolizumab was not resumed. PET-CT on POD 30 demonstrated widespread disease progression, and the patient transitioned to best supportive care. She died on POD 61 without recurrent gastrointestinal perforation, obstruction, or bleeding. Conclusions Clinically occult small bowel metastases may present with perforation or impending obstruction during systemic therapy even while previously documented lesions at other sites decrease in size. Because the intestinal lesions were not identifiable before treatment, true discordant progression could not be established. Histopathological findings supported direct tumor-related perforation rather than treatment-induced tumor necrosis or immune-mediated enteritis. Emergency source control and systematic examination of the entire small bowel may identify additional lesions that alter operative management.

title: Young-Onset Esophageal Squamous Cell Carcinoma Developing after Allogeneic Bone Marrow Transplantation for Fanconi Anemia: A Case Report.
abstract: Introduction Fanconi anemia (FA), a rare genetic disorder, is characterized by defective DNA repair and an increased risk of early-onset squamous cell carcinoma. Although hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) improves survival, long-term survivors experience a high risk of secondary malignancies, including esophageal cancer. Owing to extreme sensitivity to chemotherapy and radiotherapy, treatment of FA-associated esophageal cancer is particularly challenging. Case presentation A 22-year-old woman with FA who had undergone unrelated allogeneic bone marrow transplantation in childhood developed esophageal squamous cell carcinoma. Preoperative endoscopy, CT, and PET showed no lymph node or distant metastases, and the tumor was staged as cT2N0M0, cStage II. Because of the anticipated severe toxicity of DNA-damaging chemotherapy and radiotherapy in FA, an upfront surgery strategy was selected. Thoracoscopic subtotal esophagectomy with 2-field lymph-node dissection achieved R0 resection. Despite the absence of radiologically or macroscopically suspicious lymph nodes, histopathological examination revealed adventitial invasion, marked lymphovascular invasion, and metastases in 3 of 25 lymph nodes (pT3N2M0, pStage IIIB). Postoperative systemic therapy was considered, but its initiation was deferred because of incomplete postoperative recovery and concern regarding treatment toxicity. Multiple recurrences became evident 4 months after surgery, before systemic therapy could be reconsidered, and the patient died 10 months postoperatively. Conclusions This case highlights the therapeutic dilemma in FA-associated esophageal cancer between substantial toxicity from standard cytotoxic therapy and the risk of undertreatment with upfront surgery. The marked discrepancy between clinical and pathological staging illustrates the difficulty of excluding occult nodal or systemic disease when neoadjuvant therapy cannot readily be administered. Previous reports suggest that reduced-dose chemotherapy or chemoradiotherapy may retain antitumor activity but can still cause substantial toxicity, indicating an extremely narrow therapeutic window. Treatment therefore requires individualized multidisciplinary decision-making, while further accumulation of detailed data on treatment intensity, toxicity, response, and outcomes is needed.

title: Decreased Synovial Fluid SLC7A11 and GPX4 Levels Correlate with Knee Osteoarthritis Disease Severity.
abstract: Background Ferroptosis has been suggested to play a role in the pathogenesis of primary knee osteoarthritis (OA). The current study aimed to explore the potential relationship between the concentrations of SLC7A11 and GPX4 in serum and synovial fluid (SF) and the severity of knee OA. Methods A total of 120 patients with knee OA and 120 healthy controls were included in this study. Serum and SF levels of SLC7A11 and GPX4 were measured using ELISA before and after a comprehensive therapeutic intervention. Radiographic severity of OA was evaluated using the Kellgren-Lawrence (K-L) grading system. Clinical severity was assessed via Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) and Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoar-thritis Index (WOMAC) scores. Levels of interleukin-6 (IL-6) and matrix metalloproteinase-3 (MMP-3) were also analyzed. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was employed to evaluate the diagnostic utility of SLC7A11 and GPX4 levels in relation to K-L grades. Results Serum levels of SLC7A11 and GPX4 did not show significant differences between knee OA patients and healthy controls. However, patients with K-L grade 4 exhibited statistically significant lower concentrations of SLC7A11 and GPX4 in SF compared to those with K-L grades 2 and 3. Furthermore, SF levels of these proteins were significantly lower in patients with K-L grade 3 compared to those with grade 2. Negative correlations were observed between SF levels of SLC7A11 and GPX4 and K-L grades, as well as with SF levels of IL-6 and MMP-3. SF concentrations of SLC7A11 and GPX4 were also inversely correlated with VAS and WOMAC scores. ROC analysis indicated that both SLC7A11 and GPX4 demonstrated good diagnostic value for assessing radiographic progression in knee OA. Conclusions These results indicate that SLC7A11 and GPX4 may function as potential biomarkers for monitoring disease progression and therapeutic efficacy in knee osteoarthritis.

title: Artificial Intelligence Versus Human Interpretation in Diagnostic Radiology: A Systematic Review of Diagnostic Accuracy and Operational Efficiency.
abstract: Rising imaging workload and a shortage of radiology specialists have driven interest in artificial intelligence (AI) to improve diagnostic speed and accuracy. This systematic review, without meta-analysis, describes how AI affects diagnostic accuracy and operational efficiency compared with human interpretation in diagnostic radiology. Following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA 2020) and Cochrane guidance, PubMed, ClinicalKey, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar were searched on 11 April 2026 for studies published from January 2019 onwards. Two reviewers independently performed study selection, data extraction, and a Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies 2 (QUADAS-2)-based risk-of-bias assessment. Twenty-one studies were included: 11 compared standalone AI with human readers, six compared AI-assisted with unassisted readers, and four reported both; 18 evaluated task-specific image-analysis AI and three evaluated generative AI models. Because no subgroup was homogeneous enough to pool, we synthesised results narratively and stratified them by comparison type, AI category, imaging modality, and study quality. Standalone image-analysis AI achieved high sensitivity for fractures and selected chest findings but performed less well on subtle findings and lower-quality images, and in one computed tomography-referenced comparison a radiologist outperformed AI. AI assistance improved reader performance more consistently, particularly among less experienced readers. Generative models did not reach specialist performance on complex tasks. Efficiency gains were concentrated in normal studies, and the only randomised trial found lower mammography screen-reading workload with similar early screening performance. No study assessed patient outcomes, and 18 of 21 studies were retrospective. This evidence supports AI only as a supervised, complementary tool; improvements in diagnostic accuracy should not be equated with clinical benefit.
